newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori heads home after Peru hostage breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori heads home after Peru hostage breakthrough.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori returns home on Wednesday to direct negotiations to end a 57-day siege at the Japanese ambassador's home after a breakthrough in preliminary talks with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages.

Fujimori won British Prime Minister John Major's support for his tough handling of the hostage crisis on a visit to London to convince the business world that it was an "isolated case" that would not hurt foreign investment in Peru.

The breakthrough came from four hours of talks between the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) second-in-command Rolly Rojas and Fujimori's negotiator Domingo Palermo at a Red Cross safe house opposite the besieged residence on Tuesday.

Inside a tight security cordon of police sharpshooters and special forces, Education Minister Palermo and Rojas, who goes by the nom de guerre "El Arabe" (The Arab), met with guarantors from the Vatican, the Red Cross, Canada and an observer from Japan. Red Cross workers had erected a metal-detector at the door of the rented house to make sure no guns were taken in.

After a Red Cross car transported Rojas the 150 feet (50 meters) back to the fortified residence, the Vatican's Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent told waiting reporters both sides had agreed to further dialogue.

"Today we began the preliminary conversations. We have agreed the procedures to follow in future conversations and we have agreed to continue the conversations at a date yet to be set," said Vincent, translating Cipriani's statement.
It was the first time the MRTA and the government had come face-to-face since Palermo met the leader of the MRTA hostage- takers, Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, at the residence on Dec. 28.

The siege began on Dec. 17 when 15 MRTA rebels stormed the residence during a cocktail party and seized more than 500 guests. They freed most but kept 72 key hostages, including two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
Japan has followed the siege closely and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto met Fujimori, who is the son of Japanese immigrants, in Canada to urge him to find a peaceful solution.

Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said in Tokyo his government hoped "the talks will pave the way for the start of full negotiations so that the incident can be solved peacefully, and the hostages freed early."

Fujimori said in London he detected "elements that give us a certain optimism. (Rojas) is a sociologist familiar with the theme and he could help us find a solution." He expects the talks with Rojas, a 34-year-old former transport worker who joined the MRTA while at university, to lead to formal negotiations in the next few weeks with Cerpa himself.

Fujimori's refusal to consider Cerpa's main demand - the release of 400 MRTA rebels from Peruvian jails - had stymied earlier attempts at dialogue. He was sticking to his hard line, telling a news conference in London: "Definitely the Peruvian government is not going to pay any ransom."
He is open, however, to the possibility of asylum abroad for the hostage-takers and suggested Cuba might take them.

Cerpa Cartolini's latest comments also show negotiations are unlikely to be a pushover. "The beginning of talks does not necessarily mean the start of a solution to the conflict," he said by walkie-talkie from inside the residence on Monday, accusing Fujimori of using the talks as a "psychological weapon" and of making "veiled threat" to use force.

The threat of bloodshed has been clear throughout, beneath bizarre musical duels between police blasting patriotic "criollo" music through huge speakers and rebels chanting revolutionary hymns. The latest scare came on Monday when the rebels tossed out a grenade and fired shots to ward off police.
